articles.title: Houthis claim to have struck Saudi Aramco facility, Riyadh with missiles, drones
articles.body:
Yemen's Houthis said they attacked "sensitive" sites in the Saudi capital Riyadh on Saturday with missiles and drones, hours after flames and a large plume of smoke were seen near the city's main airport.
Saudi Arabia had sent alerts overnight warning of potential danger around Riyadh, amid an escalation in attacks by the Houthis in the kingdom.
Reuters video and photographs showed a huge pillar of black smoke rising in the area, with the airport highway, main terminal building and other facilities in the foreground. At one point in the video, flames were visible rising from behind what appeared to be fuel tanks.
The Houthis did not specify what they had targeted in Riyadh, but said they had also attacked an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key Saudi oil export hub.
The Houthis said the operation came as a response to an attack in the Yemeni capital Sanaa.
Saudi coalition reportedly defends civilian targets from missile attack
The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said its air defenses had destroyed a missile fired by the Yemeni group toward Riyadh early on Saturday.
In a statement, the coalition also said it had foiled attacks targeting civilians in the Saudi cities of Bish and Farasan in the southwest and Taif in the west, as well as Yanbu on the Red Sea coast. It did not say whether there was any damage.
Saudi civil defense sent the alerts by phone overnight for potential danger of aerial attacks in Riyadh and the city of Al-Kharj east of the capital, before issuing an all-clear on Saturday morning. A Reuters journalist in Riyadh's Olaya area heard booms before the all-clear was sent.
Although some alerts had been issued in Riyadh this year after the start of the US-Iran war, these were the first since the escalation with the Houthis began in July.
Global oil supply threatened
The Houthis, who control the most populous parts of Yemen and much of the north, have been launching attacks against Saudi Arabia since declaring a naval blockade against Riyadh in July, with strikes targeting Saudi vessels in the Red Sea.
The attacks have targeted Saudi cities, energy infrastructure and shipping, creating new threats to global oil supplies and putting at risk the main alternative Red Sea route for Gulf exports while traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains blockaded.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Saudi Arabia may have military needs due to the ongoing Houthi attacks, and Turkey was ready to help under a trilateral defense pact that also includes Pakistan.
It was unclear what kind of support Turkey might provide, but Fidan, in an interview with broadcaster NTV, said Saudi Arabia's needs could include "some technical issues."
The trilateral agreement signed last month stipulates that an armed attack on any of the three countries would be regarded as an attack on all of them.
On Friday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had foiled unspecified "criminal attempts" in the Yemeni capital Sanaa, blaming Saudi Arabia and vowing a response.
The Iran-aligned group, which seized Yemen's entire Red Sea coast in a lightning advance this month, says the Saudi Air Force has conducted hundreds of airstrikes against it in recent days.
The fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has developed as a new theater of conflict in the wider war that began with US and Israeli strikes against Iran at the end of February. US President Donald Trump has rebuffed Saudi requests for direct US military intervention against the Houthis.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told Al Jazeera in an interview aired on Saturday that Tehran wanted the war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis to end, adding that he believed Yemenis also wanted a settlement with Saudi Arabia.
Rezaei also said Iran had conveyed its conditions to mediators for re-engaging in stalled negotiations with the United States, including "ending the war on all fronts."
Consultations were continuing with Qatari and Pakistani mediators, and Tehran was awaiting a response from Trump, Rezaei said.
The UN Security Council, in a statement on Friday, "condemned in the strongest terms continued Houthi attacks against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, including attacks impacting civilian and energy infrastructure, which have resulted in the injury of civilians, including women and children."
In the statement, the Security Council also condemned "Houthi military escalation in Yemen."

articles.title: Russian Election, Cast as Test of Support for Ukraine War, Enters Final Day
articles.body:
A parliamentary election that President Vladimir Putin has cast as a test of support for Russia's war in Ukraine entered its third and final day on Sunday, with the ruling United Russia party expected to retain its dominance in a political system critics say does not tolerate dissent.
The State Duma vote, the first since Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, is likely to be presented by the Kremlin as evidence of public backing for Putin's policies and for the war, Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II, now in its fifth year with no sign of ending soon.
Most anti-war candidates were barred from the ballot. Those who did run from the liberal Yabloko party, which has polled in the single digits in recent years but hoped to tap into war fatigue, said they feared for their freedom after courts handed long jail terms to two senior party figures before the vote for comments about the conflict deemed illegal by authorities.
Discrediting the army or spreading what authorities regard as fake news are punishable by lengthy prison sentences.
The Kremlin says national unity and some censorship are necessary during what it calls its “special military operation” in Ukraine. It casts the conflict as part of an existential struggle with a hostile West and says Ukrainian intelligence services and other enemies are stepping up efforts to stir unrest inside Russia.
Putin on Friday accused Ukraine of trying to interfere in the election, citing what he said was a Ukrainian strike on the home of an election official in the Russian-controlled part of Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region that killed Yelena Astanina, the official. Reuters could not independently verify details of the attack and there was no immediate comment from Kyiv.
Russian electoral officials also said on Saturday that an online voting system in Moscow had come under cyberattack. Kyiv, which has suspended elections under martial law, has dismissed the Russian vote as a "pseudo election."
Despite what most experts see as the election's predictable outcome, the NEST think-tank in Berlin, co-founded by Kremlin critic Mikhail Khodorkovsky, whom Russian authorities have designated "a foreign agent", said the vote could still produce awkward moments for the Kremlin at a time of economic strain.
"The consequences of the war are increasingly being felt within the country, and accumulated anxiety and frustration may translate into votes for the systemic opposition parties that the Kremlin has allowed to remain on the ballot," it said in a note.
It said the Communist party and the New People party could attract votes the authorities would prefer to go to United Russia. Both parties have consistently voted in line with United Russia on major issues.
Putin told the nation in a televised address before the election that the vote would underline support for Russian troops fighting in Ukraine.

articles.title: Iran tests new anti-ship missile near US aircraft carrier
articles.body:
Iran tests new anti-ship missile near US aircraft carrier
TEHRAN — Iran has recently tested a new anti-ship missile near a US aircraft carrier, Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei said, as Tehran warned that any further US attack would trigger a stronger response against American bases and interests across the region.
In an interview with Al Jazeera, Rezaei said Iran had identified vulnerabilities in the US military and was now better prepared than before to confront American air attacks. He stressed that Iran was serious about defending itself and would strike US bases and American interests in the region with greater force if attacked.
Rezaei said the calculations and assessments made by US President Donald Trump regarding Iran and the war had been wrong, arguing that the conflict had been instigated by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
He said Washington would be better served by accepting Iran’s conditions for ending the war, adding that Trump’s threats would not produce any results and that Iran was prepared for a decisive confrontation if hostilities continued.
Rezaei said Iran had reached a conclusion to change its strategy toward Washington following the US withdrawal from a memorandum of understanding (Islamabad MoU).
He said Iran’s military had tested the new anti-ship missile near a US aircraft carrier, describing the test as part of Iran’s preparations to confront potential US attacks.
“We know the weak points of the US military and are more prepared than before to confront its air attacks,” Rezaei said.
Tehran sets conditions for ending the war
Rezaei said consultations were continuing with Qatar and Pakistan as mediators and that Iran had conveyed its conditions for negotiations to both countries.
He said Iran remained in contact with the Qatari mediator, who had relayed Tehran’s conditions to Washington for ending the war, and that Tehran was awaiting Trump’s response.
Iran’s conditions, he said, include an end to the war on all fronts, the release of frozen Iranian funds and an end to the maritime blockade.
Iran leaves NPT withdrawal as a possibility
Rezaei also said US and Israeli actions had created circumstances that could allow Iran to withdraw from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons also known as NPT.
He stressed that Iran had not planned to leave the treaty and that any such move would depend on Washington’s conduct.
“We remain committed to the fatwa issued by the martyred Leader and have not changed our nuclear doctrine,” Rezaei said, adding that Iran could not predict what might happen in the future.
Iran calls for end to Saudi-Yemeni conflict
 
 Rezaei also expressed support for an end to the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen, saying he believed the Yemenis also wanted a settlement with Riyadh.

articles.title: Russian drone strike on monastery in Kherson region kills clergy, injures 4, Zelenskyy says
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
20 September 2026•Update: 20 September 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Sunday that a Russian drone struck a men’s monastery in the Kherson region, killing a clergy member and injuring four others.

He accused Russia of launching more than 2,000 attack drones, 1,700 guided aerial bombs and 19 missiles of various types against Ukraine this week, damaging civilian infrastructure.

Zelenskyy urged Ukraine’s partners to impose new sanctions on Moscow “to enforce peace through strength.”
“The United States has the means to do this, Europe has them, and so does every G7 country. We are counting on new, strong steps,” he said.

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine trade strikes in key areas as war continues to cause heavy casualties
articles.body:
Russian and Ukrainian drone strikes reportedly killed civilians and damaged infrastructure on Sunday on both sides.
The strikes came as Russians voted on the final day of a three-day parliamentary election, while Ukraine reported deadly attacks across the Kiev and Kherson regions.
A major Ukrainian drone attack overnight on Moscow and the surrounding region killed two people and injured 20 others, Russian authorities said on Sunday.
Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said the capital came under the “most massive” drone attack, claiming more than 1,600 Ukrainian UAVs were shot down since Saturday, including 450 while approaching Moscow.
He said several drones reached the Moscow Oil Refinery, damaging the facility and one struck a residential building, with no casualties reported.
“The unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections. The adversary failed to achieve this,” Sobyanin wrote on Telegram.
Moscow Region Governor Andrey Vorobyov said on Russian social media platform Max that the attack damaged civilian infrastructure and sparked fires across the region.
The most serious consequences were recorded in the Ramensky district, where a falling drone sparked a fire on the roof of a 21-storey apartment building, prompting the evacuation of 400 people, he said, adding that 20 vehicles were damaged.
A drone also struck a three-storey apartment building in Sofyino, killing one person and injuring five others, he said. Another person was killed in the Orekhovo-Zuyevo district.
Separately, Russia's defence ministry claimed its forces intercepted and destroyed 1,110 Ukrainian drones overnight across Russia, occupied Crimea and over the Black Sea, becoming "the most massive" attack since the beginning of the year, according to state news agency TASS.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the attack, stressing “our long-range responses had a very significant impact in the Moscow region last night.”
“These are billions of dollars that sustain the war machine,” he wrote on X, adding that “sanctions were also imposed on a facility in the Voronezh region.”
Russian drone attack kills three children and a woman in Kiev region
Meanwhile, the death toll from an overnight Russian attack on the Kiev region rose to four, including three children, Kiev regional authorities said on Sunday.
A mother and her two three-year-old children were killed in Ukraine's Kiev region when a Russian drone strike hit a private home, the emergency service said.
Kiev region governor Tymur Tkachanko said a girl died in hospital after a separate drone strike in another district.
Tkachenko said the region endured more than a day of hostile attacks, with 31 sites damaged in five districts.
Russian drone strike on monastery in Kherson region kills clergy, injures four
Zelenskyy also said that a Russian drone struck a monastery in the Kherson region, killing a clergy member and injuring four others.
In a statement on X, Zelenskyy said the attack was carried out on Saturday and expressed condolences to the families and loved ones of those killed and injured.
He accused Russia of launching more than 2,000 attack drones, 1,700 guided aerial bombs and 19 missiles of various types against Ukraine this week, damaging civilian infrastructure.
Russia and Ukraine have been attacking each other with drones continually in recent weeks.

Russian forces launched a drone strike against a mobile branch vehicle belonging to Ukraine’s national postal operator, Ukrposhta, in the northeastern Sumy region on Saturday, Sept. 19, wounding postal workers inside, Ukrposhta CEO Ihor Smilyanskyi announced.
Smilyanskyi stated that Russian forces targeted the mobile postal van while employees were transporting pensions, medicines, mail, and food supplies to residents in frontline border communities.

Doctors in Sumy and Trostyanets worked overnight to treat the workers, who sustained grave trauma in the blast.

Escalating weekly bombardment across northern Ukraine

articles.title: Russia: Ukrainian drone strike on Moscow kills 2
articles.body:
Russia: Ukrainian drone strike on Moscow kills 2
September 20, 2026
Two people were killed in a Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow region, local authorities said Sunday, with an oil refinery in the region also being hit.
Energy infrastructure has been repeatedly targeted by both Ukraine and Russia, despite US President Donald Trump saying both sides had agreed to stop.
Ukraine's repeated targeting of oil refineries has led to oil product shortages and fuel price increases in Russia.
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the strike had "a very significant impact," saying the oil in the hit refinery funds "billions of dollars to sustain the war machine."
"Moscow must end its brutal war and choose peace instead of building layered rings of air defense at the expense of other regions," Zelenskyy posted on X.
According to Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin, more than 1,600 drones have been intercepted by Russia since Saturday, including 450 aimed at the Russian capital, making it one the largest Ukrainian drone attacks on the city since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Moscow mayor accuses Ukraine of trying to disrupt parliamentary election
Sobyanin said that numerous drones had made it to the oil refinery, and another one hit an apartment. The scale of the damage done to the refinery has not been confirmed.
This comes as Russia is entering the last day of its three-day parliamentary election.
Sobyanin said the "unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections."
Meanwhile, in the eastern Ukrainian, Russian-occupied region of Kherson, a drone attack on a bus had killed two people, including an election official, Russian state news agency RIA reported.
Three children killed in Kyiv region
In Ukraine, four people were killed in a Russian drone attack in the Kyiv region, local authorities said.
Among the casualties are a mother and her two 3-year-old children, as well as a girl who was taken to hospital in another district and later died.
The southwestern Fastiv district suffered damage to homes and industrial buildings.
Russia's Defense Ministry said a warehouse of drone and missile maker Fire Point was struck in the Kyiv region. It also hit a cargo vessel and a postal logistics center in the Odesa region, saying both were used for military shipments.
Russia has been repeatedly carrying out drone attacks on the Ukrainian capital in recent weeks.

articles.title: As White House shields the AI gold rush, Trump family and other allies strike it rich – with few guardrails
articles.body:
Donald Trump’s sons, through a series of AI-linked defense and technology ventures, have picked up a $620m Pentagon loan, a Marine Corps robotics contract and an undisclosed air force drone deal in the past year. His longtime friend Michael Dell won a Pentagon contract worth nearly $9bn. And this week, as public support for artificial intelligence sinks to some of the lowest levels ever recorded, the president went to bat for the industry. .
“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades,” he posted on Truth Social Monday. “There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers.” It was the first of many aggressively pro-AI posts he would make this week.
Trump is resisting new restrictions on AI at a moment when his family and some of his closest allies have accumulated financial interests in the infrastructure and defense-technology ecosystem expanding alongside the AI boom, an overlap that has now drawn scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers, government ethics watchdogs and, by some accounts, his own senior aides. It’s not clear that financial interests are driving Trump’s policy, but the two have moved in close parallel.
The administration frames its resistance chiefly as a matter of competitiveness. Trump and officials including David Sacks, who co-chairs his Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, have repeatedly argued that new rules could slow US AI development when the country is racing China for dominance of the technology. Sacks said at a Politico summit on Wednesday that recent warnings from Anthropic and OpenAI about the technology’s risks amounted to political theater, manufactured by advocacy groups and the press, and said existing laws were largely sufficient.
But many concerns are coming from inside the industry itself. In early September, Jacob Coxon – a researcher who spent three years working on the foundational training of AI models at both OpenAI and Anthropic – resigned and published a stark warning.
“Neither company is acting responsibly,” he wrote. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” He said colleagues privately believe the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade”. Anthropic’s head of AI safety, Mrinank Sharma, separately resigned the same week, writing that “the world is in peril.”
Those warnings coincided with a concrete demonstration of AI-enabled risk. A California cybersecurity firm disclosed this month that it had used artificial intelligence to build a self-spreading worm capable of hijacking WeChat accounts through a single unanswered call, and then automatically spreading through the victim’s contact list. The firm estimated the technology could compromise more than a billion devices within hours.
Tencent, the Chinese tech giant that owns WeChat, patched the vulnerability before it was deployed and said no accounts were affected, but the firm noted that building the exploit, work it said would once have taken a larger team months, took roughly 10 days with AI assistance. Around the same time, JD Vance, speaking on a Christian podcast, described certain uses of AI as carrying “really, really weird spiritual dark energy” and said there are “things about the world” that leave him “not shocked if the Antichrist was walking among us”.
Polling shows how far out of step Trump’s posture is with the public, particularly once AI’s costs become tangible. A poll released on Wednesday found just 11% of Americans support an AI datacenter being built in their own community, while 65% oppose one – including 52% of Republicans – and 57% say Trump has handled the issue of AI poorly, up seven points since March. The same day, the House voted 417-3 to require datacenters to bear the costs of the electricity-grid upgrades their operations demand, underscoring how concerns about AI’s infrastructure costs have moved from polling into Congress.
If the federal government did enact regulations that ultimately damaged AI profits, it’s possible some members of the Trump family would feel the pain. Donald Trump Jr and Eric Trump joined the investment firm Dominari Holdings last year and helped launch American Data Centers Inc, an AI infrastructure venture in which Dominari holds a minority stake. The deal came weeks after their father unveiled an expected $20bn datacenter pledge from Emirati billionaire Hussain Sajwani, and $500 bn in planned private sector AI investment, alongside an executive order unwinding Biden-era AI safeguards.
Since then, the brothers have moved from infrastructure into defense contracting, most notably through Vulcan Elements, a rare-earth magnet startup whose products are used in AI datacenters, drones and defense systems. Three months before the Pentagon announced its $620m loan to Vulcan in December – the largest the defense department’s office of strategic capital has ever issued – 1789 Capital, the venture firm where Trump Jr is a partner, quietly took a stake in the company. A ProPublica investigation found the loan request came not from Vulcan or the Pentagon but from Peter Navarro, a senior White House adviser and close friend of Trump Jr’s, and that Pentagon staff were told to move at an “unusually rapid pace”.
“The call came from the White House: We have to get this done,” one person involved in the deal told the outlet.
Trump Jr’s spokesman, the Pentagon and Vulcan have all said he played no role in the deal and that the company received no political favoritism. Eric Trump, separately, serves as chief strategy adviser to Foundation Future Industries, the robotics startup behind the $24m Marine Corps contract; senator Elizabeth Warren called that award “corruption in plain sight”. A third venture, the drone maker Powerus backed by both brothers and having signed a new agreement with Pakistan’s army, also holds a $90m air force contract, and has separately pitched its technology to Gulf states amid Iran’s striking of US bases across the region. Drones are widely expected to increasingly utilize AI technology in the coming years.
A Washington Post analysis in July found 15 companies tied to the brothers’ investment funds have generated at least $3.2bn in direct federal business since they got involved, but SpaceX and Anduril, the latter an AI-powered defense technology firm behind Lattice account for 97% of that figure, and 10 of the 15 companies already had government business before the Trump sons invested.
Excluding SpaceX and Anduril, the remaining 13 companies had received $103m in direct federal funding and nearly $1.8bn in long-term commitments after the brothers’ investments.
The pattern extends beyond Trump’s family to some of his closest technology allies. Sacks’s influence over Trump’s regulatory decisions has been substantial: in May, he reportedly persuaded the president in a last-minute call to scrap a planned executive order that would have subjected AI models to extended government review, overriding the chief of staff, Susie Wiles, and treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, who had spent months negotiating the stronger version.
His own financial position has drawn scrutiny inside the administration as a result. Sacks’s venture firm holds stakes in SpaceX and a range of AI startups, along with earlier investments in Meta, Palantir and Airbnb; federal ethics rules required him to divest only some of those holdings while he served as the White House’s AI and crypto czar, a post he left in March. Some administration officials have privately looked into whether Sacks could personally benefit from blocking new AI rules, the Wall Street Journal reported.
The outlet reported that Musk pushed in the same direction, joining Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang last month in personally lobbying Trump against a proposed industry-funded AI oversight body, helping shelve the plan. Dell, a member of Trump’s science and technology advisory council and a longtime friend and donor to the president, saw his company win the nearly $9bn Pentagon contract in May, prompting ethics watchdogs to question whether his advisory role created an unaddressed conflict.
The technology industry is not uniformly aligned behind Trump. Federal filings on OpenSecrets show the broader communications and electronics sector still sends roughly two-thirds of its political money to Democratic candidates and committees this cycle. Trump’s support among industry figures has come instead from a narrower group: OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Greg Brockman have given tens of millions of dollars to a pro-Trump super Pac and Trump’s inaugural committee, though have also donated to Democrats in the past.
The Pentagon’s own account of its safeguards makes no distinction between a routine contractor and a company whose investors include the president’s son, which is a gap Democratic lawmakers asked the Pentagon’s inspector general to investigate last month.
Next week, Trump is set to host the leaders of the country’s leading AI companies at the White House, a meeting arranged with the House speaker, Mike Johnson, that will coincide with a visit from the Chinese president, Xi Jinping.
In the meantime, the investments continue.

articles.title: Houthis fire ballistic missile at Riyadh, US fears rapid escalation
articles.body:
AA Photo
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis fired a ballistic missile at the Saudi capital Riyadh on Sept. 20.
 The Saudi-led coalition intercepted and destroyed the missile before it could hit civilian targets.
 Shrapnel scattered across several residential neighborhoods in the capital.

 The United States warned of a rapid escalation in the Middle East following the strike.

articles.title: Slovak PM Fico says some in West seek war between Russia and NATO
articles.body:
Slovak PM Fico says some in West seek war between Russia and NATO
MOSCOW – Some Western politicians are seeking conflict between NATO and Russia after a “failed” strategy to defeat Moscow in its war with Ukraine, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said on Sept 19.
Long-time Slovak leader Fico, who has kept up warm relations with Russia and refuses military aid for Ukraine, said this week that Europe was closer than ever to a large-scale war erupting from the Ukraine war.
At the same time, some European leaders, such as those in France and Poland, have warned of Russian hybrid attacks.
In his video message, Fico said, “We face a mortal danger” while watching the West “pour fuel on the fire” with its support for Ukraine, which he said had been to no avail.
“The failure of the strategy to destroy Russia through the war in Ukraine has led some Western politicians to believe that if the goal cannot be achieved through the Ukrainian army and full support for it, then every effort must be made to trigger a conflict between NATO and Russia,” Fico said in the video posted on social media.
He said the war in Ukraine was not Slovakia’s nor NATO’s war but said, “Certain war hawks within NATO are trying, at any cost, to turn this war into a conflict between Russia and NATO.”
Earlier this week, Fico warned a drone incursion could spark the activation of NATO’s collective defence clause and he wanted to prevent Slovakia - which neighbours Ukraine and is a member of the NATO military alliance - from becoming part of an armed conflict.
He said on Sept 19 that creating a pretext to start a war was easy and reiterated Slovakia would not send soldiers to fight under a fabricated pretext.
French President Emmanuel Macron said on Sept 18 that Russia was intensifying its campaign of hybrid attacks against Europe, and he cited an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport in August, which the German government concluded Moscow was behind, as evidence of the changing nature of Russian aggression.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Sept 17, citing unnamed intelligence agencies, that Russia plans to launch hybrid drone and missile attacks against countries supporting Ukraine. REUTERS

articles.title: AI, Middle East escalation, Ukraine-Russia war on agenda for upcoming UN General Assembly
articles.body:
World leaders gather in New York this week for the UN General Assembly, bracing for US President Donald Trump's return to the rostrum for a second year running, with talks centering on the widening conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine and the risks of artificial intelligence.
Nearly 130 heads of state meet with the post-World War Two order under strain and with the UN itself struggling to remain relevant and weathering attacks from Trump, who has slashed America's contributions and withdrawn from dozens of UN bodies.
Chinese leader Xi Jinping, who last addressed the diplomatic jamboree via video in 2021, will skip New York in favor of one-on-one talks with Trump in Washington on Thursday, fueling debate about the UN's relevance in addressing global crises.
Compounding the crisis of morale and finance are questions about the next leader of the 80-year-old organization: Secretary-General Antonio Guterres completes his term at the end of 2026, with no clear frontrunner in the race to replace him.
The 15-member UN Security Council may hold high-level meetings on Ukraine, AI, and the Middle East, including talks with Arab leaders, diplomats said.
More than a year into Trump's second term, "we would no longer say that the UN is in freefall, but we would say that it's stuck in an open-ended crisis," said Richard Gowan of the International Crisis Group.
"The UN may not be in emergency care like it was last year, but it seems to be trapped in a trauma center for the foreseeable future," Gowan said.
The US avoided losing its vote at the assembly by paying $725 million in contributions to the regular budget this week, but it still owes the organization more than a billion dollars and makes ongoing demands for cuts and reforms.
AI leaders call for slowdown on development
The assembly meets shortly after several artificial intelligence industry leaders called for a coordinated slowdown of the development of the technology, warning that it could soon improve on its own and escape human control.
Guterres has said that AI will be a major topic, adding that countries pushing its frontiers should set up "common guardrails in order to avoid this race to the bottom that could lead one day to a gigantic disaster at the global level."
The secretary-general has long proposed global governance of AI. In 2023, the UN created an advisory body on the technology, with members including tech executives, government officials and academics.
The warning has put Guterres at odds with Trump, who dismissed AI risks as a "hoax," saying there is a "sick conspiracy" against it and that China would benefit from the doubt being cast on its development.
War in Iran, Houthi attacks key issues in Middle Easy talks
The Middle East will again be a focus of discussions, as the US-Israeli war on Iran continues to drive global inflation and destabilize the region. Recent gains by Houthi terrorists threaten shipping in the vital Bab al-Mandab Strait and could further spike energy prices.
"It's very difficult to have a military solution for that problem, and the experience of fighting in Yemen demonstrated how complicated it is to have successful interventions," said Guterres, adding that the UN's envoy on Yemen was making a "huge effort" to advance talks.
Peace talks remain stalled, however, as Iran and the US continue to exchange strikes and Trump threatens a major escalation of the war.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the assembly on Wednesday.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court and will reportedly face protests following his arrival, is due to speak on Thursday.
Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas will for the second year running not be at the gathering in person. The US, a close Israeli ally, again denied him a visa. On Thursday, the General Assembly voted to allow Abbas to appear via video.
There is likely to be a high-level meeting on the conflict in Sudan on the sidelines, diplomats said, although a diplomatic breakthrough is unlikely.
Zelensky seeking to improve Ukraine's position before winter
Also on the agenda is Russia's more than four-year-old war in Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov will address the General Assembly. Zelensky will likely seek to shore up Ukraine's position ahead of what is expected to be another tough winter, diplomats said.
The Security Council has been unable to take action to end the conflict because permanent member Russia holds a veto.
Trump has at times appeared frustrated that he has been unable to broker an end to the war, a goal he declared a priority when he began his second term in January last year. The US president spoke with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin earlier this month, but it was unclear whether he plans to meet Zelensky in New York.
Guterres highlighted the impact the war was having on civilians but also on food security and energy prices.
"The effective blockade existing in the Black Sea is creating enormous problems that add to the problems generated by the Middle East crisis, and I think it would be very important to find a way to allow Ukrainian exports and Russian exports of food, fertilizers and energy to take place in a safe way through the Black Sea," he said.

articles.title: JP Morgan admits it can't forecast end of Iran war due to Trump
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
JP Morgan admits it can't forecast end of Iran war due to Trump's flip-flopping
JP Morgan has said that it is unable to forecast the end of the US war with Iran, in an admission that its own assumptions about the war's dynamics have not held up.
"For the first time since the start of the Iran conflict, we don't have a baseline view. We simply don’t know how to model the endgame," the bank's global commodities team said in a note published on Thursday.
This is because the underlying assumptions about US President Donald Trump's own red lines, which in theory would limit the war's duration, have not held up.
These include $100 oil, $5 a gallon of petrol, and 4% inflation or 5% yields on 10-year Treasuries, US government bonds that it sells to prop up government spending.
"Those constraints gave us an implicit timeline, and we expected that by June there would be some form of agreement to reopen the strait," the note said, adding that all of these have failed to compel the Trump administration to end the war and ensure the Strait of Hormuz reopens.
Since the start of the Iran war, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has dramatically affected the global commodity market, with 20% of the world's oil and gas entering the global market through the key waterway.
The price of oil has dramatically fluctuated as oil exports slumped at the immediate start of the war, then picked up as alternative export routes were found, including Iraqi exports via land through Syria, Saudi Arabia's diversion through its East-West Pipeline, the UAE's diversion through its Fujairah pipeline, and a US initiative to smuggle out oil via the strait, bypassing Iranian attacks.
Yet, struggles to export oil have continued as Iranian attacks still threaten maritime shipping, and the reignition of the Yemeni civil war sees Houthi attacks against Saudi oil infrastructure.
"With no clear signals from either the US or Iran that they are prepared to de-escalate… the assumption that the disruption is temporary is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain," JP Morgan's note read.
Has Trump and the war affected economic forecasts?
Jamie Brito, the Executive Director in Refining & Oil Markets at Dow Jones Energy, told The New Arab that the situation is "everybody's energy nightmare. What everybody had feared for the last decades came to fruition this year".
"We are on uncharted territory. Every single analyst team is in uncharted territory. It's quite difficult to predict this kind of, you know, extreme scenario," he said.
Brito said his team's forecasts were based on its observations and analysis of trade, oil production, refining, and other key nodes in the market. Many teams look at these nodes for their own forecasts.
He added that key signposts can be used to understand where things may change, including this summer's World Cup in the US, Canada and Mexico, the establishment of the Memorandum of Understanding between the US and Iran in June, as well as the upcoming midterm election in the US, which is the next signpost.
Trump's rhetoric, however, is increasingly being dismissed in forecasts.
"What we are acknowledging, or what people are seeing, I think is the fact that you cannot expect, you cannot wish or anticipate that the political arena is going to be forced to capitulate or to accept some kind of negotiation and ceasefire, because of some political pressure," Brito said.
What does JP Morgan’s admission mean?
Trump's messaging, and that of his administration, has flip-flopped since the start of the outbreak of the war with Iran.
Initially saying the war would be short, his administration fumbled on its justifications for launching the war. It gave differing reasons for launching the war, including aiming to stop Iran from getting nuclear weapons, regime change, and has even threatened to destroy the country despite seeking negotiations with it.
Trump's most recent prediction for the war is that it would end after the midterms.
Neil Quilliam, an associate fellow with Chatham House's Middle East and North Africa Programme specialising in energy policy and geopolitics, told The New Arab that the admission from JP Morgan is less a statement that its team, or the industry, expects the war to get worse or of a worse economic outcome, but that "some of the assumptions underpinning its forecasting framework no longer hold".
"Assumptions that analysts would ordinarily use to construct an endgame have become much less reliable, and may remain so for the remainder of the Trump administration," he added.
Quilliam said that Trump's statements, and the fact that they don't necessarily reflect the administration's policy on the ground, cause an "unusually challenging environment" for businesses and markets to navigate, which make it difficult for forecasters to establish a baseline for investment decisions.
JP Morgan's statement, he said, is more an admission that "the range of plausible outcomes [of the war] has widened while confidence in assigning probabilities to them has collapsed".
"This is an arguably more significant admission. Markets can price known risks. They find it much harder when there is no reliable framework for judging which outcome is most likely," Quilliam said.
This, in turn, has knock-on effects for economic decision-making.
"Business can still plan around a range of scenarios, but attaching confidence to a single base case becomes increasingly difficult when the political decision-making driving the crisis remains so unpredictable."

articles.title: No meeting can force Iran to surrender
articles.body:
No meeting can force Iran to surrender
Siasat-e-Rooz examined the meeting of senior military commanders from the United States, Israel, and several Arab countries in Germany, writing that Arab states are currently facing a major crisis: the collapse of their security-building strategy based on US presence and, in some cases, normalization with Israel.
This reality became clear not only during the Ramadan War but also in recent developments in Yemen. Although these states have previously formed coalitions with the US, making this nothing new, the key point is that the Berlin meeting will ultimately not change regional equations. Such a gathering will neither improve regional security nor reduce tensions; instead, it will intensify them and further contribute to the tightening of the Strait of Hormuz. Arab countries that rejected the Oman meeting cannot now expect the Berlin meeting to force Iran to surrender or reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Therefore, before becoming trapped in a difficult situation, they should abandon the illusion of an American security umbrella and take steps toward localized security alongside Iran.
Shargh: Why has China entered the Hormuz file?
Shargh evaluated the importance of the Strait of Hormuz for China. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi considers reopening the Strait of Hormuz essential for stabilizing energy transport and preventing the crisis from spreading to Yemen and the Red Sea. Beijing’s motivation is not merely political. China has long been the largest buyer of Iranian oil, and any disruption in Persian Gulf energy exports directly affects its economy. Thus, when Wang Yi speaks about reopening Hormuz, there is a clear economic and security concern behind his position. Attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and pressure on the Bab al-Mandab route have expanded the crisis from a single strait to a network of vital energy corridors. As a result, Beijing can no longer treat Hormuz as merely an Iran–US issue; each day of continued crisis makes the energy and trade implications more serious for China.
Hamshahri: The map of Middle East trade routes
Hamshahri wrote that disruptions in shipping caused by the Iran–US war have pushed Middle East countries toward roads, railways, pipelines, and even new fiber‑optic routes, reshaping the region’s trade map. The war has challenged the region’s historic dependence on maritime routes. Disruptions in ship traffic through Hormuz have ushered in a new phase of regional trade—one in which roads, railways, land borders, pipelines, and even alternative sea routes have become core elements of economic security. At the same time, recent events—such as the attack on Saudi Arabia’s East–West pipeline—show that even alternative oil routes are not immune to war. Thus, the issue is not simply replacing Hormuz; the conflict is exposing the vulnerability of an entire chain of regional corridors. The new transformation in the Middle East is therefore not just the revival of land routes but a simultaneous competition and reconfiguration among multiple trade and energy corridors.
Sazandegi: The JCPOA is still alive
Sazandegi analyzed Thursday night’s event at the UN Security Council, where China and Russia vetoed the US draft resolution against Iran. The incident shows the JCPOA can still influence Iran’s legal and political dynamics. Russia and China vetoed the US resolution to extend the mandate of the Iran sanctions expert panel by citing the very clause in the JCPOA and Resolution 2231 that outlines the termination of Iran’s file at the Security Council. For this reason, the Islamabad understanding should be taken more seriously, and efforts should be made to implement it. The issue is not merely the text of an Iran–US understanding; it is about creating a pathway for resolving disputes—especially given that both countries have experienced the costly consequences of withdrawing from agreements and returning to confrontation. The veto by Russia and China once again revealed the divide among permanent Security Council members over the legacy of the 2015 nuclear deal.
Farhikhtegan: Why BRICS matters for Iran
The composition of BRICS shows clearly that it is not a unified bloc. Russia, facing Western sanctions, has adopted firmer positions toward the West. China seeks to avoid confrontation, and India does not want BRICS to be defined as anti‑Western. Nevertheless, a large portion of Iran’s economy depends on interactions with BRICS members. China, the UAE, India, Brazil, and Russia are among Iran’s main partners—and all are BRICS members. Emphasizing national currencies and creating alternatives to SWIFT can reduce much of the impact of unilateral sanctions. Beyond economics, the West has tried for at least two decades to isolate Iran diplomatically, but BRICS membership has undermined that strategy. Another reason BRICS is important is its ability to prevent anti‑Iran statements: since Iran is a member and final communiqués require unanimous approval, no anti‑Iran statement will be issued within BRICS.

articles.title: US approves potential $2.68B air defence package for Ukraine
articles.body:
The United States has approved a potential $2.68 billion sale of air defence equipment to Ukraine, after Kiev made repeated pleas for support to fend off Russian attacks.
The State Department said on Friday in a congressional notification that it made "a determination approving a possible foreign military sale to the Government of Ukraine" for buying air defence development upgrades and related equipment and services.
Kiev has requested to buy equipment including multiple types of missiles, launchers, counter-drone radars and trailers, according to the State Department.
The proposed sale is subject to congressional review.
"If the proposed purchase is concluded, Ukraine would finance it using a combination of European contributions and US Foreign Military Financing appropriated during the prior administration," the State Department said.
US President Donald Trump said this month he would ask Europeans to repay the American aid provided to Ukraine under the administration of his predecessor Joe Biden.
Trump has long demanded that Europeans shoulder more of the cost of Western support for Ukraine.
Friday's proposal, which the State Department estimated would cost $2.68 billion, came as Trump signed a bill authorising new sanctions designed to squeeze Russia.
Middle East war hampers peace efforts
Ukraine's capital Kiev has seen a surge in Russian attacks, which its air defences have struggled to repel due to ammunition shortages.
Moscow is seeking to drain Ukrainian morale and intimidate Kiev's European allies at a time when the Kremlin believes it has the advantage in weapons production, analysts say.
The war in the Middle East has also hampered US-mediated talks on ending the conflict, taking up much of Washington's time and munitions.
But even before that conflict, which broke out in February, Russia and Ukraine remained at odds over the key issue of territory.
Ukraine has proposed freezing the conflict along the current front lines.
Russia has rejected this, saying it wants the whole of the Donetsk region, despite it being partly controlled by Ukraine, a demand Kiev says is unacceptable.

articles.title: US overreliance on AI contributed to deadly Iran school strike – Bloomberg
articles.body:
US overreliance on AI contributed to deadly Iran school strike – Bloomberg
Heavy reliance on AI, staff cuts, and rushed targeting procedures contributed to a US missile strike on an Iranian girls’ school in Minab, Bloomberg reported on Friday, citing officials involved in a Pentagon investigation.
On February 28, two Tomahawk missiles hit the Shajarah Tayyebeh Elementary School in southern Iran, killing at least 157 people, including 123 children. The strike took place during the opening wave of US and Israeli attacks across the country. The school stood across from a naval base, which was likely the intended target.
Some US Central Command (CENTCOM) personnel reportedly expected Palantir’s Maven Smart System to flag stale or inconsistent intelligence when selecting potential targets. Previous reports suggested that the military relied on outdated satellite imagery that depicted the school as part of the base.
According to Bloomberg, Maven allowed the process of assembling target lists to be condensed to just several minutes.
A Palantir spokesperson told Bloomberg that the company was “not responsible for the underlying data nor identifying intelligence deficiencies” and that there was no evidence its software was at fault in the Minab strike.
The AI giant has since upgraded Maven to “re-review underlying intelligence to identify factors that would disqualify a target and flag inconsistencies and inaccuracies that human review may have missed,” Bloomberg said, citing a person familiar with the matter.
Investigators also reportedly noted that, under orders from Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, the Pentagon dismantled most of its civilian harm mitigation (CHM) units and cut their staff by around 90%, to fewer than 20 people. A CHM team at CENTCOM was reportedly reduced from ten people to one, and no CHM official reviewed the Minab site before the strike.
UN Human Rights Chief Volker Turk said at the time that the bombing of the school “evoked a visceral horror.” On Thursday, a UN fact-finding mission said there were “reasonable grounds” to believe that the strike constituted a war crime. The US State Department rejected the finding, accusing the UN of pushing “anti-American rhetoric and anti-Semitism” and appeasing “repressive regimes.”
The US has not publicly acknowledged responsibility for the strike, with President Donald Trump suggesting that the missile could have been Iranian. However, investigations by US media outlets suggest that the missiles were American.

articles.title: North Korea launches apparent ballistic missile into Korean Peninsula sea, Japan says

North Korea launched what appeared to be a ballistic missile into the sea to the east of the Korean Peninsula on Sunday, Japan's defense ministry said.
South Korea's defense ministry said the rival North had fired an unidentified projectile. Japanese public broadcaster NHK said it had come down outside Japan's exclusive economic zone.
Only hours later, North Korea fired a second missile off its east coast, local Yonhap News outlet reported.
A day earlier, North Korea dismissed a resolution by the UN nuclear watchdog against Pyongyang's nuclear program, in a statement through state media.
North Korea condemns US-Japan-South Korea naval drill
Pyongyang last week also condemned a US-led naval drill including South Korea and Japan, which ran from August 29 to September 10 near Guam.
North Korea's Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of leader Kim Jong Un, on Friday blamed US-led military drills for "ever-worsening" tensions on the Korean Peninsula and vowed no change in the country's course to strengthen its nuclear arsenal.
South Korea’s presidential office convened a National Security Council (NSC) meeting on Sunday following the reports of North Korea's launch of short-range ballistic missiles into the East Sea from the Wonsan area.
Condemning the launch, the second in about a week following a previous test on September 12, the NSC urged Pyongyang to immediately cease missile activity, warning that the test directly violates United Nations Security Council resolutions.

Amnesty International had previously reported that Russia’s recruitment of foreign nationals into its armed forces relies on deceptive, coercive, and exploitative practices that in many cases amount to human trafficking under the UN’s Palermo Protocol.

articles.title: Trump vows not to slow AI despite industry warnings
articles.body:
Trump vows not to slow AI despite industry warnings
US President Donald Trump has vowed not to slow the development of AI despite warnings from leading technology executives about the potential risks posed by increasingly powerful systems.
Trump also announced the creation of an ‘AI Force’ and said he would appoint an AI czar, while pledging to maintain America’s lead over China in the rapidly developing technology.
“We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry,” he wrote on Truth Social on Saturday. “Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!”
Trump accused his political opponents of seeking the “decimation, or destruction” of AI, describing the push as the latest in a series of hoaxes generated by “Radical Left Dumocrats.” He argued that abuses of the technology can be addressed through the justice system.
“For this purpose, I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term,” Trump wrote, referring to the sixth branch of the US armed forces, established by Congress in 2019 to conduct military operations in space and protect American assets such as satellites.
Trump also said he would soon announce an AI czar, adding that “only High I.Q. individuals need apply!” He did not provide details about the proposed force’s composition, powers, budget, or position within the federal government.
The US president described AI as potentially more consequential than the Industrial Revolution and the internet, and predicted that it could eventually account for as much as 25% of US GDP. “We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!” he wrote.
Trump’s position contrasts with warnings from prominent tech executives. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI chief Sam Altman, SpaceX and xAI chief Elon Musk, and Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis have backed calls to slow the development of increasingly powerful AI systems.
Last week, Amodei warned that rapidly advancing systems could escape human control, be misused for cyberattacks and bioterrorism, and cause serious economic disruption. Anthropic Alignment Science lead Evan Hubinger estimated there is a greater than 10% chance that AI could “kill all humans” within the next decade.
Trump has dismissed concerns that AI could take over the world as a “hoax,” and hailed AI and data centers as the “greatest economic development engine in history.”
Earlier this week, Bloomberg reported that flawed military intelligence, outdated imagery, and overreliance on AI contributed to a strike in February on an Iranian school that killed more than 150 people, including at least 123 children.

articles.title: Australian premier urges US, China to strike deal on AI's rapid development
articles.body:
Aamir Latif

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on Sunday called upon the US and China, the two leading nations in the artificial intelligence (AI) race, to strike a deal on the technology. 
Albanese made the call during a visit to the headquarters of the tech giant Apples in Cupertino, California on his way to New York to attend the UN General Assembly session next week, as the US President Donald Trump steps up his fight against regulation.
He urged Washington and Beijing to cooperate and strike a deal similar to the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, signed in 1970 to stop the spread of nuclear weapons.
"The truth is they're the big two giants here and so we want to see cooperation," he said.
Albanese said he would be speaking to like-minded leaders at the upcoming UN General Assembly session, for global rules to regulate the AI's rapid development.
Describing AI as a "global phenomenon," Albanese said that sitting on the sidelines was not an option.
"There is a need for a discussion about what the global framework is for the rollout of AI, because it is moving very quickly, and we need to make sure that humans remain in control," he added.
The fresh debate over the pace of AI development was triggered after Anthropic chief Dario Amodei called for a coordinated slowdown. His call was backed by OpenAI's Sam Altman and SpaceX's Elon Musk.
Trump, however, has pushed back on the call, arguing any deceleration would give America's biggest competitor, China, the upper hand.
Ahead of his upcoming summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House, Trump doubled down on his argument, declaring he would establish a new "AI Force" to protect against the "decimation or destruction" of AI.

Israel demands 'compensation' from US after Saudi F-35 sale
Israel is demanding compensation from the US after being notified of its intention to sell F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, according to Israeli news outlet Walla.
The State Department said Thursday it had approved the sale of 48 planes to Saudi Arabia in a deal worth $24.3 billion.
Israel has long opposed the sale of the advanced aircraft to other countries in the region to preserve its technological superiority.
The US has so far only allowed the sale of F-35s to its closest allies, including a number of European NATO allies and Israel, which is currently the only country in the Middle East with access to F-35s.
After being informed of the Saudi deal, Israel is demanding the US agree to provide it with weapons it has so far refused to sell it, the Israeli outlet reported, citing an anonymous Israeli official.
The official did not disclose which weapons it has requested.
It is also demanding it be allowed to participate in the development and production of classified weapon systems.
US officials said this week they are planning to deliver tens of thousands of heavy 2,000-pound bombs to Israel as part of an upcoming arms deal.
Saudi Arabia and other countries in the region have long sought to purchase F-35s, which are advanced fifth-generation stealth fighters.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pressured Trump not to sell the aircraft to Turkey, which entered talks with the US over a potential deal earlier this year.

articles.title: Thousands of IRGC, Basij volunteers march through Tehran in show of defiance against US, Israel
articles.body:
Hundreds of thousands of Iranians participated on Friday in a rally organized by the regime in Tehran, in the largest display of defiance of its kind since the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.
Participants said they were prepared to take up arms and defend the country after months of war and a worsening economic situation in Iran, the Associated Press reported.
The rally was held as part of an initiative called “Janfada Iran,” meaning “those who sacrifice their lives for Iran.” Participants marched through central Tehran in combat uniforms and carried flags, while crowds along the streets cheered them on. Some protesters stepped on US and Israeli flags and chanted “Death to America” and “Death to Israel.”
In the days before the rally, state media called on the public to join the initiative and announced that limited training in the use of assault rifles would soon begin.
The volunteers are intended to serve as an additional layer of defense alongside the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Basij militia, which has played a central role over the years in suppressing protests against the regime.
Tehran IRGC commander General Hassan Hassanzadeh told state television that more than 600,000 people had already registered for the program and that the regime expects more than 1 million people to participate in training. Iranian television estimated that more than 300,000 people took to the streets of the capital on Friday, although the figures could not be independently verified.
Basij head says recruits will be 'nightmare' for Iran's enemies
The new head of the Basij, Hossein Taeb, announced at the opening of the rally that the volunteers would be ready for “comprehensive defense” and that similar events would soon be held in additional cities. He said the new recruits would become a “nightmare” for Iran’s enemies.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, military commanders, and other senior regime officials watched the parade.
“I came to tell Trump that we Iranians are not afraid of his threats against our homeland,” said Marzieh Afaghi, 24, who attended the rally with her husband and young child. “No one throughout history has managed to invade Iran and remain there.”
The rally also served as an opportunity for the regime to display military equipment. Air defense systems were deployed on the streets, and female IRGC fighters wearing black head coverings were seen alongside machine guns mounted on vehicles.
The IRGC also displayed drones of the type used in attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran claims responsibility for tanker attack in Strait of Hormuz
At the same time as the events in Tehran, Iran claimed responsibility for an attack on the oil tanker Trend, sailing under the flag of Togo.
According to state television, the tanker was targeted because of what it described as an “illegal attempt” to pass through the Strait of Hormuz.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said a vessel was struck by a projectile and that a fire broke out onboard, which was later extinguished.
According to UKMTO, the number of vessels passing with US military assistance off the coast of Oman averaged 24 per day over the past week. However, overall maritime traffic in the area remains about 90% lower than in the period before the war.
Iranian attacks and threats in the strait have severely disrupted oil and natural gas shipments from Gulf countries to markets around the world.
Expanded Basij enables greater suppression of future protests
According to AP, the recruitment initiative also has domestic significance: expanding forces aligned with the Basij could strengthen the regime’s ability to suppress future protests.
In January, shortly before the outbreak of the war, Iran saw some of the largest nationwide demonstrations in the country’s history. The protests began over the economic crisis and expanded into calls against the government.
Human rights activists claimed that more than 7,000 people were killed in the crackdown on the protests and that tens of thousands were arrested.
In May, government officials claimed that more than 30 million of Iran’s roughly 90 million residents had volunteered through an online form or at public events to sacrifice their lives for the regime.

articles.title: Two civilians killed as Ukrainian drones strike homes near Moscow
articles.body:
Two civilians killed in Moscow suburbs as Ukraine launches ‘unprecedented’ attack during elections – officials
Two civilians were killed and several others, including two children, were injured in Moscow Region during a powerful Ukrainian drone raid that was aimed at derailing Russia’s parliamentary elections, local officials said.
In a statement on Sunday, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said more than 1,600 UAVs were repelled since the previous day, adding that 450 UAVs were intercepted on approaches to the capital.
“The unprecedented attack was clearly planned to disrupt the elections. The enemy failed,” he said.
Several drones reached the premises of the Moscow Oil Refinery, where one unidentified facility was damaged, and one struck a residential building, according to Sobyanin, who said there were no fatalities in the capital.
The consequences of the raid, however, were much more destructive in the suburbs. Earlier in the day, Moscow Region Governor Andrey Vorobyov reported damage in the Ramenskoye District, southeast of Moscow, where a 44-year-old woman was killed and five others, including two children, were injured when a drone hit an apartment building in the village of Sofyino.
In the nearby city of Ramenskoye, around 400 people, including 70 children, were evacuated from a 21-story apartment block after falling drone debris sparked a fire on the roof, with 20 vehicles also damaged.
Another person was killed in the Orekhovo-Zuyevo District, where a private home was destroyed and caught fire during the attack. The victim was an elderly man who was inside the building, according to the governor.
Elsewhere in Moscow Region, a warehouse complex caught fire in Sofyino, and a drone struck an apartment building in Kotelniki, setting apartments on three floors ablaze. The authorities are still determining whether anyone was injured.
Private homes were also damaged in Kolomna and Yegoryevsk, while fires broke out at apartment buildings in the Leninsky District, Lyubertsy, and Lytkarino. A residential building and an industrial facility were damaged in Istra, with no casualties reported.
The massive raid struck Moscow and the surrounding region just hours before polling stations were due to open for the final day of Russia’s three-day parliamentary elections. Despite the attack, all 1,443 polling stations in Moscow opened on time, Moscow Election Commission Deputy Chairman Dmitry Reut told TASS.
Moscow has accused Kiev of undermining diplomatic efforts while publicly calling for renewed negotiations. On Friday, Russian President Vladimir Putin said the Ukrainian leadership is “talking about peace” while doing everything to prevent peace and negotiations.
Earlier this month, Putin ordered large-scale retaliatory strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure in response to attacks inside Russia. Moscow has condemned the strikes on civilians as acts of terrorism, while maintaining that Russian forces only target military and defense-related facilities.

articles.title: ‘Russophobic West’ to blame for lost Ukraine peace chance – NATO state leader
articles.body:
‘Russophobic West’ to blame for lost Ukraine peace chance – NATO state leader
Ukraine made a “huge mistake” by caving in to its Western backers and walking away from a potential peace deal with Russia in 2022, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has said. He also argued that years of Western military backing have failed to defeat Russia and are now raising the risk of a direct clash between Russia and NATO.
In a video address posted on X on Saturday, Fico argued that both sides have sustained “terrible” losses over the years, and that Western military support has failed to contain Russia’s advances. “There is no supranational force to compel Russia to withdraw from the militarily controlled Ukrainian territory,” he said.
“Ukraine made a huge mistake in April 2022, a few months after the start of the conflict, by listening to the Russophobic West and not signing the prepared peace agreement,” he said, adding that the Western strategy “to support the war in Ukraine to the last Ukrainian soldier and defeat Russia” has “completely failed.” He reiterated that his government will not provide military assistance or loans to Ukraine.
Confronted with the failure to destroy Russia through the Ukraine conflict, “several politicians in the West… believe that if it cannot be achieved through the Ukrainian army and its full support, everything must be done to provoke a conflict between NATO and Russia,” Fico stated.
“Someone must have gone crazy here,” he said, arguing that “Russia cannot be defeated in a conventional war” and noting that it has a vast nuclear arsenal.
Fico stressed that the Ukraine conflict is “not a NATO war,” arguing that “only some war hawks in NATO are trying at all costs to turn this war into a conflict between Russia and NATO.”
He noted that the Slovaks had their own experience with the Munich Agreement in 1938, saying that “the powers bound to us by treaty deceived us, betrayed us, and served us up to Hitler like a roasted chicken.” The Munich Accord – which was a prelude to World War II – was signed by Nazi Germany, Britain, France, and Italy without Czechoslovakia at the table and compelled Prague to surrender the predominantly German-speaking Sudetenland.
In spring 2022, Russia and Ukraine made substantial progress toward a peace deal, including a tentative draft agreement on Ukrainian neutrality, security guarantees, and other core issues.
Russia accused then-UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson of helping derail the peace process, which he has denied. Ukrainian chief negotiator David Arakhamia later confirmed that Johnson played an influential role. He said Russia was prepared to end the conflict if Kiev accepted neutrality, adding that Johnson told Ukrainian officials, “We won’t sign anything with them at all, and let’s just fight.”
While the peace settlement process intensified after US President Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, no breakthroughs have been achieved. In February, the Russian Defense Ministry said Ukrainian military casualties exceeded 1.5 million since 2022, including more than 520,000 in 2025 alone.

articles.title: New US sanctions law undermines Ukraine peace efforts – Kremlin
articles.body:
New US sanctions law undermines Ukraine peace efforts – Kremlin
The sanctions law signed by US President Donald Trump this week will undermine efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict through diplomacy, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said.
On Friday, Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which authorizes tougher restrictions on Russia and tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
“Clearly, this cannot have a positive effect,” Peskov told RIA Novosti on Saturday when asked how the law would affect the prospects for a peaceful settlement in Ukraine and the possibility of a breakthrough in Russia-US relations.
Named after the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine who co-authored the original bill with Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal in 2025, the legislation remained stalled for months as Trump pursued diplomacy with Russia and resisted placing sole blame for the conflict on Moscow. Trump’s envoys also discussed normalizing economic ties with their Russian counterparts.
The Senate passed the measure 86-11 last month, followed by the House on Wednesday in a 262-159 vote.
The original proposal threatened tariffs of 500% on countries purchasing Russian energy, but the maximum rate was reduced to 100% after negotiations with the White House. Graham, who died unexpectedly in July, promoted the measure as “bone-crushing” sanctions.
The version adopted by Congress targets major buyers of Russian oil and gas, with China and India expected to be among those potentially affected. It also gives Trump broad discretion over the application of the tariffs, including the ability to waive or suspend restrictions in the national interest.
Peskov previously described the bill as an “unfriendly action” that would “complicate efforts to find a peaceful settlement in Ukraine.”
The Russian Embassy in the US said the legislation does “a grand disservice” to Trump’s ‘Make America Great Again’ agenda, arguing that restricting Russia’s energy trade amid sharply reduced Middle Eastern supplies could send fuel prices soaring ahead of the midterm elections. It warned that confrontation with Russia and China is a lose-lose situation that only benefits the “Euro-Atlantic warmongers.”
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun condemned the law, saying China “carries out economic and trade cooperation with countries on the basis of equality and mutual benefit” and that its trade is not directed against any third country.
